events.excerpt: You can’t expect ATOM’s price to rise significantly while inflation continues to dilute holders and new tokens keep entering the market. Lower inflation. Fewer new tokens. A well-designed burn mechanism. Stronger real demand. These are the changes Cosmos needs to restore confidence in ATOM. Technical upgrades are important, but if they don’t translate into real demand for ATOM, what is the point? Holding ATOM must become genuinely attractive. The token needs stronger utility, and the growth of the Cosmos ecosystem must finally translate into value for ATOM holders. Cosmos has the potential, but potential alone is not enough. We need concrete decisions and measurable results. Without meaningful tokenomics reform and sustainable demand, ATOM risks continuing to underperform, even if the ecosystem keeps growing. It’s time to stop making promises and start delivering results. ATOM deserves better. 5 posts - 4 participants Read full topic

events.excerpt: Our jobs as developers are changing. In a couple of years, we’ve gone from writing every line of code to working with AI assistants to orchestrating fleets of agents. But the goal hasn’t changed: ship completed software work. A feature, a bug fix, a security fix. Completed work, not more code, is the output that matters. Today at GitHub Universe , we shared our vision for GitHub as the most comprehensive software delivery system in the world. We introduced products that bring that vision to life and showed how we’re rebuilding the infrastructure underneath it. Our vision: From idea to completed software The SDLC is no longer a linear path from planning to coding to testing to deployment. A code change, a request from a colleague, or a production metric can trigger work anywhere in the system. Most of us (and our agents) jump between different stages, depending on the task at hand. Developers set the direction, make decisions, and stay accountable for what ships. Agents implement and verify changes. And everything feeds into and out of a continuous learning machine that makes the next cycle better. This agentic software delivery system solves for three things: Velocity: get from idea to completed software as quickly, efficiently, and cost-effectively as possible Intelligence: comb
events.headline: GitHub Universe 2026: Evolving every layer of the stack

events.excerpt: Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the past 12 months, more than in 2024 and 2025 combined. Behind that number are developers building what interests them and what their communities need. In Nepal, one developer built a flood bulletin on GitHub Pages with verified information on roads, rescue, weather, and power. It has since grown into Gati , a Nepali-first relay of official disaster alerts that runs on GitHub Pages and Actions. Elsewhere, developers at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory are creating software designed to run programs aboard spacecraft , and fans built open-source firmware that lets people customize their e-readers . Curiosity, aimed in every direction, at a scale GitHub hasn’t seen before. That growth happened quickly. Partway through the year, activity on GitHub bent sharply upward, just as agents went from something developers were trying out to something they were working alongside. Developers picked from more models than ever and built in industries we are highlighting in this report for the first time, from health care to agriculture. Octoverse is our chance to step back and look at the whole picture. This year, that picture is bigger than ever. Here is what stood out most: More AI, more of everything. Among repositories created this year,
events.headline: Octoverse: Commits, pushes, reach new highs in 2026 as developers build with agents

events.excerpt: Two threads here this month made me look at the same problem from both ends. In one , a holder has ATOM on UX Chain, which halted in July, and RoboMcGobo explained why the Hub can’t just release it: the escrow only opens when the other chain burns the voucher, and that chain makes no blocks. In the other, Akash’s proposal 346 (voting until 2 November) starts a migration that ends with akashnet-2 halting 90 days after a later cutover. So I went through ibc-go (v10.7.0, the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs; akashnet-2 runs v10.5.0, and the transfer code I cite is the same there) to list what has to happen before the last block, because after it nobody can fix anything from the other side. This is not about whether any chain should leave. It’s only about the tokens. Why tokens get stuck When a token leaves its home chain, it goes into that chain’s escrow for the channel and the other side mints a voucher. The escrow releases it only when a packet shows the voucher was burned, and that packet has to come from a live chain. Transfer channels can’t be closed. The transfer module rejects ChanCloseInit , so there is no close-and-settle step. Every packet, ack and timeout is checked through the counterparty’s light client, and the client has to be Active. events.excerpt: Ephemeral Rollup: The New “L1.5” of Ethereum TLDR; Ethereum’s core job has always been verifying state transitions. While rollups made that verification succinct, they at the same time hold their users’ state, which is why every rollup needs an exit. Native account abstraction ( EIP-8141 and related EIPs) and proof aggregation are making it practical to keep compute and state apart. We call this L1.5 , albeit it is perhaps more an architectural pattern than a layer. In the pattern we are talking about: a) The wallet keeps the user’s own state, b) L1 keeps the shared state and verifies every transition, and c) the compute in between is done by whoever takes the job without holding any state the next job needs, and d) state changes settle directly on L1. The idea is not new: Relayers, builders and keypers have already done parts of this kind of job, and FOCIL’s includers will be next. What is new is the timing, “now and next”, as this becomes practical to build. We aim only to give a rough conceptualization of it in this post. Introduction Ethereum first verified state transitions by re-executing them. Rollups added succinct verification, where a fraud or validity proof lets L1 accept a batch without re-executing it. But a rollup also holds its users’ state. The state is kept in th
events.headline: Ephemeral Rollup: The New "L1.5" of Ethereum

TL;DR Zyfai would run up to 10M USDC from the SLL, rebalanced daily across USDC lending venues on Ethereum, including Spark Blue Chip USDC. Two risk tiers, chosen by Spark. Over the last 90 days, net of a 5% Zyfai fee, Spark’s margin over the Sky Savings Rate would have been: conservative: 96 bps, 1.7x Spark Blue Chip USDC (57 bps) aggressive: 278 bps, 4.9x Spark Blue Chip USDC On 10M per year: about $96k (conservative) or $278k (aggressive), against about $57k from Spark Blue Chip USDC. Spark keeps custody: the Safe is owned by SPARK_PROXY . Zyfai can only move funds between allowlisted venues or back to the ALM Proxy. No controller change: inflow uses the existing transferAsset path with a 10M rate limit. 1. Why The SLL earns the difference between venue yield and the Sky Savings Rate (SSR). Spark Blue Chip USDC is today Spark’s direct USDC allocation on Morpho: about 19.6M, almost all from the ALM Proxy, in two markets (cbBTC 86% LLTV about 85%, wstETH 86% LLTV about 15%). events.excerpt: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event. In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters. Disruptions at a glance Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq,
events.headline: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026

events.excerpt: Update — October 30, 2026: Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections. Details of managed-rule changes are available in the Cloudflare WAF changelog . The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the Cloudflare HackerOne program. We will share further information and feedback as the challenge progresses. Thank you again for your contributions. Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised , creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell : serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web. Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. Nobody, including operators, can link answers to people. Every voter can verify their own recorded ballot. Anyone can recount the result from public data. Full disclosure first: most of the current design and code was drafted with a team of AI agents, disclosed in AGENTS.md. None of it has been reviewed by independent humans yet. That is why I am posting. Design in brief Enrolment, document. The phone reads an ICAO 9303 passport chip over NFC. It proves in zero knowledge that the chip data was signed by a document signer in a public tree of checked signers, without revealing the document. The signers are checked against a published trust list of country signing certificates. The list holds references only and has a hash anyone can rebuild. The first version is built from the German master list: 113 of 186 chip-passport countries. Enrolment, person. The live face is matched to the chip photo inside an attested enclave. events.excerpt: Author: @adust09 from Nyx Foundation Abstract In this post, we will take stock of the challenges facing PQ P2P in the consensus layer. Ethereum consensus-layer networking has no adopted post-quantum migration profile. Replacing validator BLS signatures with leanXMSS does not update the networking identities and handshakes used by ENRs , Discovery v5 , libp2p Peer IDs, or QUIC/TLS. The migration has three linked targets: Discovery: ENR signatures, Discovery identity proofs, and Discovery key exchange. Connection key exchange: TLS 1.3 key agreement inside QUIC. Connection authentication: libp2p TLS identity binding and TLS CertificateVerify . The main constraints are structural: an ENR is limited to 300 bytes, a Discovery packet to 1,280 bytes, and hybrid key exchange does not provide PQ authentication. In practice, hash-based signatures are being promoted for consensus signatures, but the size limits of the P2P layer make lattice-based schemes the de facto standard candidates for networking. This inventory maps the required changes without selecting an algorithm, encoding, or activation schedule. This article is intended for developers working on the network layer and libp2p. Please feel free to send me your feedback. 1. Scope This post covers Ethereum CL networking over libp2p an
events.headline: Inventory of PQ P2P Migrations in the Consensus Layer

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, I’m Samuel, building Privara, a privacy-focused payment protocol on Stacks. We’ve completed our initial grant milestones and deployed a working mainnet payment flow. I’m now exploring how to extend its privacy model, particularly around selective disclosure. What’s implemented Privara currently uses secp256k1-based stealth-address derivation to generate one-time recipient addresses, reducing the ability to link payments through a persistent recipient address. The implementation also includes SIP-018-based payment authorization, sponsored transaction flows, and payment discovery mechanisms. These provide recipient-address privacy, not full transaction confidentiality. Amounts, transaction activity, and other on-chain metadata remain observable. What I’m exploring The next step is payment-scoped selective disclosure: allowing a recipient to share verifiable information about a specific payment with an auditor or counterparty without exposing unrelated payments or granting access to their entire wallet history. I’m considering a design where a recipient can generate a narrowly scoped disclosure package containing payment-specific evidence, potentially supported by encrypted payment metadata and cryptographic proofs. This is still research, not an implemented viewing-key
events.headline: Privara: Exploring payment-scoped selective disclosure for privacy on Stacks

events.excerpt: On September 8, 2026, we were alerted by a security researcher, Gadi Evron from Knostic , to a tenant isolation issue affecting the GLM-5.3 Workers AI model ( @cf/zai-org/glm-5.3 ) starting on August 27, 2026. We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. Between August 27 and September 9, a small number of customers using the GLM 5.3 Workers AI model received responses that contained data from other customers' requests made to the same model shortly before theirs. In total, 155 responses were affected, all to prompts longer than 681,280 tokens. After excluding our own testing and the researcher's, the requests we identified are consistent in timing and volume with ordinary long-context use, not with someone repeatedly exploiting the bug. We found no evidence of deliberate exploitation. Today we are publishing this report alongside a post from SGLang, the open-source inference engine that we use, as a coordinated disclosure. This post describes the bug that caused this issue, our response timeline, and the subsequent hardening we have conducted on our production SGLang deployments. We also detail our continued efforts with the upstream maintainers of SGLang to address this and simil

Release v5.21.0 New Model additions MiniCPM-OCR MiniCPM-OCR is a document-understanding model from OpenBMB's MiniCPM-V family. It keeps the MiniCPM-V 4.6 architecture, which pairs a SigLIP vision encoder and a window-attention merger with a Qwen3.5 language model. It is specialized for reading text-dense images such as scanned pages, screenshots, receipts and tables. Links: Documentation | Paper Feat test ( #49920 ) by @guarin in #49920 Flint Flint is Recursive's mixture-of-experts language model. Compared to a standard SwiGLU MoE transformer such as Qwen3-MoE, it uses hybrid attention (sliding-window attention with rotary embeddings over the current token and the previous 512 tokens in most layers, and full attention without positional encoding in the remaining layers). It also has learned attention sinks, as in GPT-OSS, with per-head RMS-normalized queries and keys. Each sparse layer routes a token to 6 of 256 experts by sigmoid score and adds an ungated shared expert, and the first two layers are dense. Links: Documentation Add Flint model support. events.excerpt: Since Prague, execution-layer requests for validator exits and partial withdrawals go through a 504-byte contract at 0x00000961Ef480Eb55e80D19ad83579A64c007002 , hand-written for the geas assembler. At the end of every block the protocol makes a system call to it, and that call is consensus-critical: EIP-7002 requires a block whose call fails to be invalidated. We proved two properties of the deployed runtime bytes in Lean 4: The system call always succeeds, whatever the contract’s storage holds, and uses at most 210,000 of the 30,000,000 gas it is given. Requests leave in exactly the order they arrived. Over any valid history since the contract’s deployment, the committed submissions are exactly the emitted withdrawal requests followed by the entries still queued. Both are stated against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing, also written in Lean, and cover the Prague, Osaka, BPO1 and BPO2 forks. The proofs use no axioms beyond Lean’s standard three: propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound . Before deployment, the contract had already been examined by four audits and a loop-bounded Halmos check . The results here connect the deployed bytes to Jaune’s block processing, with exact gas, and follow requests from submission to delivery across histories. The
events.headline: Lean verification of EIP-7002: system-call success and FIFO requests

events.excerpt: Protocol This release introduces protocol version 39 On devnet , this protocol version can be enabled no earlier than 2026-10-26 18:29 UTC (start of epoch 3). Please ensure that you update your validators before this epoch change. Otherwise, if the upgrade threshold is reached, the protocol will remove you from the committee, and both you and your delegators will lose rewards. #13131 : From protocol version 39 on devnet and testnet, random beacon DKG that misses its timeout round keeps running and can enable randomness again mid-epoch instead of disabling it for the rest of the epoch. #13169 : Protocol version 39 enables consensus_dedup_only_recorded_messages on all chains. A consensus message is skipped as a duplicate only of an earlier message with the same key that was recorded as processed or, in the same commit, passed verification, so all validators reach the same decision about a later copy of a dropped message. #13300 : Raise the minimum validator joining stake to 6M IOTA, the low stake threshold to 5.5M IOTA and the very low stake threshold to 5M IOTA. #13285 : From protocol version 39, a multisig whose committee mixes Ed25519 with other key schemes is only accepted when every committee member has signed. #13308 : groth16::prepare_verifying_key and groth16::verify_groth1

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, I’m Maxim from Timeus Lab, the team behind Atomic Launchpad. We’re deploying it to Arbitrum One this week, and before we do, we’d like to introduce it here and hear from delegates. What it is Atomic Launchpad lets anyone launch a token for 0.0005 ETH. Tokens trade on a bonding curve. When the curve fills, it graduates into its own Uniswap v4 pool, and the liquidity position is locked permanently. Two things set it apart: A graduation bar that starts low. For the first 72 hours after deployment, a token graduates at 0.01 ETH raised. After that, the bar rises every 4 hours, up to 4.2 ETH by day 30. Early creators get the cheapest path to a real pool. Creators earn on every trade. Each trade pays a 1% base fee, and a creator can add up to 10% on top, fixed at launch. Creators keep 70% of the fee, and the protocol keeps 30%. Why Arbitrum One DefiLlama lists 11 launchpads on Arbitrum. Together they earned less than $2 in fees over the last 30 days ( DefiLlama , checked October 26). A creator who wants to launch a token on Arbitrum One today has no live place to do it, so they launch on other chains and take their communities with them.
